blocks.text: Defence mechanisms are not descriptions; they are explanations for certain human behaviour and experiences, so they are part of explanatory psychopathology.
These defences operate both in normal individuals and under pathological conditions.

Anna Freud organised the Freudian defences; Klein and later contributors added more. Vaillant (1977) classified and categorised them into mature, immature and neurotic defences. Kleinian defences are sometimes called psychotic defences.
Using a narrow repertoire of defences repeatedly, and repeated use of immature or neurotic defences, may be associated with disease states or traits.

blocks.caption: Flowchart titled 'How is a defence mechanism formed?': Wish or Impulse (double-headed arrow with Prohibitions (moral, social or legal)) -> Signal Anxiety -> Defence operation -> Symptoms formed.

blocks.text: Repression is the primary defence is the correct statement to spot. The wrong options all overreach: defences operate only in pathological situations, all defences lead to complete resolution of anxiety, acting out is a mature defence, immature defences are characteristic of psychosis. The explanation says defences develop in the course of normal maturation.

blocks.text: Altruism: using constructive and gratifying service to others to receive a vicarious satisfaction, without giving up one's pleasures. It is distinguished from altruistic surrender, in which surrender of direct gratification of instinctual needs takes place to satisfy the needs of others to the detriment of the self.

Humour: comedy is used to express feelings and thoughts overtly without personal discomfort and without producing an unpleasant effect on others; it allows the person to tolerate and yet focus on troublesome aspects.

Anticipation: realistic planning for future inner discomfort, with mental preparation for the worse. Anticipation without a specific target or goal is nothing but free-floating anxiety and is not helpful; the mechanism is goal-directed and implies careful planning for potential difficulties.
Sublimation: achieving impulse gratification only after altering a socially objectionable impulse to a socially acceptable one. It allows instincts to be channelled, rather than blocked.

Suppression: consciously or semiconsciously postponing attention to a conscious impulse or conflict. Issues may be deliberately cut off, but they are not avoided; discomfort is acknowledged but minimised.

Intentional blocking of recall (this is **NOT** unconscious forgetting - contrast from repression)

blocks.text: Neurotic defences act at the level of mental inhibition. The patient is deprived of some degree of freedom in decision-making, but retains insight.

Displacement: interest and/or emotion is shifted from one object onto another less-threatening, often less-retaliating one. Example: one told off by her consultant during clinical supervision may displace the anger onto her spouse or dog.

Dissociation: temporarily but drastically modifying one's sense of personal identity to avoid emotional distress. Fugue states and hysterical conversion reactions are common manifestations. It may also be found in counter-phobic behaviour (a person with fear of heights takes up parachute diving and experiences dissociation during the act).
Isolation: splitting or separating an idea from the affect that normally accompanies it but is now repressed. Noted in **OCD**.

Rationalisation: offering rational explanations to justify attitudes, beliefs or behaviour that may otherwise be unacceptable; the underlying motives are usually instinctually determined. It often involves finding excuses when self-esteem is threatened, and is often seen in teenagers and those who abuse alcohol and drugs.

Reaction formation: transforming an unacceptable impulse into its exact opposite. It is characteristic of obsessional neurosis but may occur in other neuroses. If used frequently at an early stage of ego development it can become a permanent character trait, as in an obsessional personality.

Repression: expelling or withholding from consciousness an idea or feeling. Primary repression curbs ideas and feelings before they have attained consciousness; secondary repression excludes from awareness what was once experienced consciously. Repression is the primary defence; other defences reinforce it.

Intellectualisation: excessively using intellectual processes to avoid affective expression or experience - needless emphasis on the inanimate to avoid intimacy with people, attention to external reality to avoid expressing inner feelings, and emphasis on irrelevant details to avoid perceiving the whole. It is closely allied to rationalisation but, unlike rationalisation, is not an attempt to substantiate one's instinctual impulses.
Identification with the aggressor: seen where the victim of aggression begins to assume the qualities of the proponent of aggression.
Undoing: seen in **OCD** and associated with magical thinking and rituals. Example: a student who thinks that tapping his table three times before the exam means he will surely succeed.

blocks.text: A detained patient who shouts at the new cleaner but not at the doctor or social worker who committed him is displacement (redirecting feelings from an object that gives rise to anxiety to a safer one). Reaction formation, denial, projection and splitting were the distractors.

blocks.text: Projection and denial are often called narcissistic defences, though some authors dispute this and regard them as immature defences.

Projection: perceiving and reacting to unacceptable inner impulses as though they originated outside the self. For example, a person who attributes hostility to others may be unconsciously projecting their own hostility; internal threats become externalised and are easier to handle.
Denial: the explicit refusal to acknowledge a threatening reality. It may persist despite constant explanation of the facts, and is not the same as conscious avoidance of painful topics or thoughts.

blocks.title: Narcissistic defences: conflict, result and process
rows: Ideas of reference, prejudice, suspiciousness, injustice
Attributing one's own feelings to be coming from others
Stubborn and angry negation of reality that is visible to onlookers
Refusal to acknowledge the awareness of reality; disavow problems at unconscious level

blocks.text: Narcissistic personality maps to projection, not projective identification, which is the tempting neighbouring option; the explanation defines projection as attributing one's own unacceptable ideas and impulses to an external target.

blocks.text: Paranoia is linked to projection: Freud linked it to the paranoid personality, defending against unacceptable impulses, especially hate and aggression. Undoing, denial, reaction formation and isolation were the distractors.
Same unconscious thought, two defences. 'I hate him' (unconscious) with 'He hates me' (conscious) is projection: the impulse is denied and attributed to someone else.
'I hate him' (unconscious) with 'I don't hate him' (conscious) is denial, not projection, reaction formation or sublimation: the forbidden thought is actively denied.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. Mock 7 explanation: denial is a refusal to accept external reality because it is too threatening, and is commonly used by people with severe physical illnesses (a man with bilateral below-knee amputation who talks about the weather instead of his illness).

bullets.text: Projection and denial: called narcissistic defences (some authors call them immature).
Projection: unacceptable inner impulses perceived as originating outside the self; internal threat externalised.
Projection results: ideas of reference, prejudice, suspiciousness, injustice.
Denial: explicit refusal to acknowledge a threatening reality despite explanation; not conscious avoidance.
Q3: projection is the defence most often used in narcissistic personality.

blocks.text: Splitting: seen most often in those with borderline personality. Qualities of an object or person are split into black and white - either good or bad, with no grey area in between.

Idealisation and denigration are often accompanied by splitting in those with borderline traits: an object is either glorified and supremacy ascribed (idealised, omnipotence ascribed) or considered very negatively and cursed (denigration). Psychiatrists treating such patients often experience phases of both.

Projective identification: an aspect of self is projected onto someone else. The projector influences the recipient to identify with what has been projected, and the projector now believes the aspect originated from the recipient, so the recipient may behave in a manner similar to the projector. It may be seen in psychotic paranoid states.

blocks.title: Ogden's three steps of projective identification
rows: Projection of a part of oneself onto an external object (step 1a is the blurring of self and object representations, which may or may not be seen)
An interpersonal interaction in which the projector actively pressures the recipient to think, feel and act in accordance with the projection
Reinternalisation of the projection after the recipient has psychologically processed it

blocks.text: The notes add that step 3 is absent while step 2 is not necessary to define 'projection'.
Projective identification has manifold aims: it may be directed toward the ideal object to avoid separation, or toward the bad object to gain control of the source of danger.

Various parts of the self may be projected: bad parts in order to get rid of them as well as to attack and destroy the object; good parts to avoid separation, to keep them safe from bad things inside, or to improve the external object through a kind of primitive projective reparation.
Introjection: internalising the qualities of an object. It is seen in normal development too.

Omnipotence: the original Freudian description is the belief that one can transform or influence the external world through one's thoughts alone. Seen in **OCD** (e.g. a woman with depressive obsessions who is distressed because she thinks something will actually happen to her baby due to her thoughts).
Grandiosity: Klein's description pertains to manic defence, closely associated with narcissism.

blocks.title: Kleinian defences: conflict, result and process
rows: Overwhelming experience of negative qualities of oneself or positive qualities of others
Stripping off either all positive or all negative qualities of others
Ideas of reference, prejudice, suspiciousness, injustice
Converting own hostile impulses to justifiable reactions to the hostility expressed by others
Internalising the qualities observed in an external 'object' e.g. mother, friend
Attaching great value ('power') to thoughts and believing they can influence external objects

blocks.text: Projective identification, not projection, is the answer when A projects impulses onto B and B unconsciously behaves as if the projection were true. In projection one perceives someone else as feeling the same way; in projective identification one causes the other to feel that emotion.

blocks.text: Immature defences are mostly normal in early phases of development and do not essentially convey abnormality.

Acting out: the expression of an unconscious wish or impulse through action to avoid being conscious of an accompanying affect. The unconscious fantasy is lived out impulsively in behaviour, thereby gratifying the impulse instead of prohibiting it.
Passive aggression: expressing aggression towards authorities indirectly through passive obstructive activities - e.g. procrastination and taking sick leave to 'defeat' one's boss.
Somatisation: converting psychological states and tension to bodily symptoms.
Regression: moving back into a childish or earlier developmental phase to avoid confronting a conflict. It is also considered an essential concomitant of the creative process.
Somatosensory amplification: the tendency to experience bodily sensations as unusually intense or distressing, thought to underpin somatisation and the somatoform disorders.

sections.title: 8. Dynamic models of the mind: topographical theory

blocks.text: The topographical theory was elaborated in The Interpretation of Dreams in 1900. The mind is divided into three regions: the conscious, preconscious and unconscious systems.

The functions of these regions are based on one of two principles. The pleasure principle is the innate tendency to avoid pain and seek pleasure. The reality principle is a learned function which requires delay or postponement of wish fulfilment according to environmental reality.

blocks.title: The three systems of the topographical theory
rows: Receives and processes information from the outside world; contents communicated via speech and behaviour; attention cathexis (investment of psychic energy on an idea or feeling to process it consciously); operates mainly secondary process thinking

As-and-when-needed service; interfaces with both unconscious and conscious (unconscious contents become conscious by 'squeezing' through it); maintains the 'repressive barrier' to censor unacceptable wishes and desires (not the repressed contents)

Contains censored or repressed wishes; characterised by primary-process thinking; governed by the pleasure principle; shift of cathexis happens often and quickly; evident via parapraxes (Freudian slips) and dreams

blocks.text: The repressive barrier that censors unacceptable wishes is maintained by the preconscious system (it interfaces with both unconscious and conscious regions), not by the unconscious system, conscious system, id or superego.

blocks.text: Conscious, subconscious and preconscious are **NOT** the structural model; they are topographical regions. The true statement in that question is that the id functions through primary process thinking.

blocks.text: The ego is governed by the reality principle, not the pleasure principle. The ego is not the most primitive part of the personality and spans conscious, preconscious and unconscious.

blocks.text: Problems with the topographic theory: when someone employs defences such as displacement or repression they are not aware of the process, so these cannot be represented by the preconscious as Freud thought (the preconscious is available to the conscious as and when needed). An unconscious need for punishment was frequently noted among Freud's patients, which the topographical theory fails to explain.

blocks.note: Notes give no account of the structural model. **Q18** explanation: in the structural model the infant mind comprises the id (entirely unconscious, wishes to pursue its own desires regardless of morality or external reality), and as development occurs the mind further differentiates into the ego and then the superego.

sections.title: 9. Instinct/drive theory and hierarchy of anxiety

blocks.text: Instinct/drive theory derived most of its terms from biology; drive and instinct are often used interchangeably.

blocks.title: Four principal characteristics of an instinct
rows: Part of body where the instinct originates
Action directed towards the discharge of energy/tension

blocks.text: Dual instinct theory holds that sexual energy and aggressive energy are the dual instincts. Libido is the force by which the sexual instinct is represented in the mind and can be considered part of Eros. Aggression is an instinct with destruction as aim, originating in skeletal muscles, and can be considered part of Thanatos.
Eros and Thanatos are the life and death instincts respectively. According to Freud, the dominant force in biology is Thanatos.

blocks.title: Hierarchy of anxiety
rows: Unconscious perception of external or internal threat leads to resource mobilisation and aversion of threat; forms the basis of defence mechanisms
Concerns about fusion with an external object
When mother is recognised as an independent object
Fear of object loss / loss of love
Especially in girls at phallic stage
Mature form of anxiety - id vs ego conflicts

sections.title: 11. Dynamic interpretation of dreams: Freud's route to dreams

blocks.text: Freud was initially trained as a neurologist. Joseph Breuer and Freud together treated Bertha Pappenheim (Anna O.), after which hypnosis became a psychoanalytic technique. Freud later used the cathartic method of abreaction - recovering and verbalising suppressed feelings that cause the symptoms.

Freud encountered patients who could not recall significant memories and called this resistance. He proposed resistance was caused actively by largely unconscious forces involved in repression, leading to symptom production. This made him abandon abreaction/catharsis and pursue free association, where patients are allowed to speak their mind without censor.

Patients often reported dreams during free association; Freud noted dream content was closely related to repressed memories and the unconscious and declared dreams the 'royal road to the unconscious'. By his wish fulfilment theory, dreams are attempts to fulfil unconscious wishes in a surrogate manner.
The content of dreams may include nocturnal sensory stimuli (e.g. thirst, hunger), the daytime residue (thoughts and ideas from waking life), and repressed impulses.

blocks.title: Manifest vs latent dream content
rows: What is recalled by the dreamer
Unconscious thoughts and wishes that threaten to awaken the dreamer

blocks.text: The unconscious mental operation by which latent content is transformed into manifest content is called the dream work.

Dream work converts **LATENT** content into **MANIFEST** content; the reversed option (manifest converted into latent) is the distractor. Primary process thinking does occur in dreaming and dreams are not always interpreted.

sections.title: 12. Dream work mechanisms and process thinking

blocks.title: Mechanisms of the dream work
rows: Several unconscious impulses are combined into a single image in the manifest dream content (e.g. one's father and the horrible teacher unified as a single dreadful monster in a child's dream)
The converse of condensation: multiple images in dreams represent one unconscious impulse
Transfer of energy from an original object to a symbolic representation of it; includes transfer of affective energy (cathexis) on the substitute, not merely forming an alternate substitute

blocks.text: Condensation is combining various unconscious impulses into a single image. The other options describe symbolic representation (abstract concepts by recognisable images) and displacement (transfer of energy to a symbolic representation).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/6) Dynamic Psychopathology Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Symbolic representation: highly charged objects or abstract concepts are represented by innocent images that are in some way connected with the original object (e.g. a dream of intense dancing may represent a desire to attract a colleague sexually).
The mechanisms of condensation, displacement and symbolic representation characterise primary process thinking, which defies logic and lacks a sense of time and space.
Primary process thinking can accept the presence of contradictory items simultaneously and is often incoherent; it is the modus operandi of the id.

A more mature aspect of the ego helps organise primitive aspects of dreams more coherently; this is secondary revision. The process by which it occurs is secondary process, which is logical, with intact time and space boundaries, and mature.

blocks.title: Primary process vs secondary process
rows: Defies logic; often incoherent; accepts contradictory items simultaneously
Lacks a sense of time and space
Modus operandi for the id; characterises condensation, displacement and symbolic representation
Mature; the process by which secondary revision occurs

blocks.text: According to Freud, anxiety dreams reflect a failure in the protective function of the dream-work mechanisms.
Punishment dreams defy the wish fulfilment theory; Freud explained them as a compromise between conscience and repressed wish, the wish for punishment being supposed to exist as an unconscious wish.

bullets.text: Condensation: several unconscious impulses merged into one manifest image.
Irradiation/diffusion: converse - many images for one impulse.
Displacement in dreams: transfer of energy and cathexis to a symbolic substitute.
Symbolic representation: charged objects shown as innocent connected images.
Primary process (id): illogical, no time/space sense, accepts contradictions, incoherent.
Secondary revision (mature ego) organises dream; secondary process is logical with intact time/space.
Anxiety dreams = failure of dream-work protection; punishment dreams = compromise between conscience and repressed wish.
